_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Argentina covering Cueva de las Manos cave art, Diaguita-Calchaquí civilizations, Inca Kollasuyu expansion, Spanish colonization (Buenos Aires founded 1536/1580), Jesuit Missions, Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata 1776, May Revolution 1810, San Martín liberation, civil wars (unitarios vs federales), Rosas dictatorship, Generation of '80 (Belle Époque), Perón/Evita, Dirty War 1976-83 (30,000 disappeared), Falklands/Malvinas War 1982, democratic restoration, 2001 economic collapse, and Kirchner era to Milei.

religion.note: Historically strongly Catholic (Pope Francis is Argentine, first Jesuit and first Americas pope); secularization accelerating; Evangelical growth; Jewish community (~250,000, largest in Latin America); AMIA bombing 1994; Muslim minority

ethnic_groups.name: European descent (White)
ethnic_groups.notes: Massive European immigration 1880-1930 (Italian, Spanish, also German, Polish, Ukrainian, Welsh); 'Italy's southernmost city'; Buenos Aires cosmopolitan; gaucho mixed culture; porteño identity

ethnic_groups.name: Mestizo
ethnic_groups.notes: Mixed European-Indigenous; more common in northern provinces (Salta, Jujuy, Tucumán); historically undercounted

ethnic_groups.name: Indigenous
ethnic_groups.notes: Mapuche (Patagonia), Guaraní (northeast), Wichí, Qom/Toba, Diaguita; Conquest of the Desert 1878-85 (genocide); land rights activism

ethnic_groups.name: Arab descent
ethnic_groups.notes: Syrian and Lebanese ('turcos'); Carlos Menem was of Syrian descent; significant commercial influence

ethnic_groups.name: Afro-Argentine
ethnic_groups.notes: Historically larger population; decimated by wars (used as front-line soldiers), yellow fever 1871, assimilation; under-recognized; recent diaspora from Africa/Caribbean

ethnic_groups.name: Asian and Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Chinese, Japanese, Korean communities; Jewish (culturally significant)

country_profile.notes_unique: Second largest country in South America; tango (Buenos Aires, UNESCO intangible heritage); Patagonia; Iguazu Falls; Peronism (unique political movement, neither left nor right); Evita (Eva Perón, icon); Dirty War 1976-83 (military junta, ~30,000 desaparecidos, Mothers of Plaza de Mayo); Falklands/Malvinas War 1982 (vs UK, Argentina lost); 2001 economic collapse (5 presidents in 2 weeks); Messi (greatest footballer); Pope Francis (Jorge Bergoglio); chronic inflation; beef/asado culture; Patagonian Welsh colony (Y Wladfa)

current_leader.name: Javier Milei
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: Libertarian; La Libertad Avanza party; chainsaw-wielding campaigner; radical austerity; dollarization advocate; anarcho-capitalist; economist; outsider; slashed ministries

former_leaders.name: Alberto Fernández
former_leaders.notes: Peronist; Cristina Kirchner as VP (real power); COVID lockdowns; economic crisis; inflation >100%

former_leaders.name: Mauricio Macri
former_leaders.notes: PRO (centre-right); businessman; market reforms; $57B IMF loan; economic difficulties; Boca Juniors president

former_leaders.name: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner
former_leaders.notes: Peronist; wife of Néstor; populist; nationalizations (YPF); corruption convictions; assassination attempt 2022

former_leaders.name: Néstor Kirchner
former_leaders.notes: Peronist; post-crisis recovery; human rights trials for Dirty War; defaulted debt restructuring; died 2010

former_leaders.name: Eduardo Duhalde
former_leaders.notes: Interim; managed post-2001 crisis; devaluation; temporary stabilization

former_leaders.name: Fernando de la Rúa
former_leaders.notes: UCR; resigned during December 2001 crisis (helicopter escape); economy collapsed

former_leaders.name: Carlos Menem
former_leaders.notes: Peronist; neoliberal reforms; peso-dollar peg (convertibility); privatizations; corruption; AMIA bombing 1994; Syrian descent

former_leaders.name: Raúl Alfonsín
former_leaders.notes: UCR; restored democracy after Dirty War; Trial of the Juntas 1985 (historic); hyperinflation forced early departure

former_leaders.name: Military Junta (Videla, Viola, Galtieri, Bignone)
former_leaders.notes: Dirty War; Proceso de Reorganización Nacional; ~30,000 disappeared; torture; death flights; Falklands/Malvinas War 1982 (Galtieri); convicted of crimes against humanity

former_leaders.name: Juan Domingo Perón
former_leaders.notes: Peronism founder; labour/social reforms; Evita; overthrown 1955 (Revolución Libertadora); 18 years exile; returned 1973; died in office 1974; wife Isabel succeeded (first female president)

910.name: Pre-Columbian Peoples of the Southern Cone
910.description: The diverse indigenous civilizations inhabiting present-day Argentina from the earliest Paleo-Indian settlers through the complex societies that existed prior to Inca expansion — including Cueva de las Manos rock art, Diaguita city-builders, Guaraní agricultural communities, Mapuche pastoralists, and nomadic Pampas and Patagonian peoples.

sub_clusters.name: Earliest Inhabitants and Paleo-Indian Sites
sub_clusters.description: The earliest human occupation of Argentina, evidenced by sites such as Los Toldos and Piedra Museo in Patagonia. The Cueva de las Manos (Cave of the Hands) in Santa Cruz province contains stunning rock art dating to c. 7300 BCE, one of the most important prehistoric art sites in South America.
key_events: Cueva de las Manos rock art created c. 7300 BCE — UNESCO World Heritage Site
Los Toldos and Piedra Museo — earliest Patagonian settlements c. 11000 BCE

sub_clusters.name: Diaguita-Calchaquí Civilization of the Northwest
sub_clusters.description: The Diaguita (including the Calchaquí, Quilmes, and Huarpe) of northwestern Argentina built fortified settlements (pucarás), developed irrigation agriculture, created distinctive ceramic and metalwork traditions, and organized complex chiefdoms in the Andean valleys. The Quilmes pucará held up to 5,000 inhabitants.

sub_clusters.name: Guaraní and Littoral Peoples
sub_clusters.description: The Guaraní inhabited the Mesopotamian region (Entre Ríos, Corrientes, Misiones) with sophisticated slash-and-burn agriculture, producing manioc, maize, and yerba mate. Alongside them, Chaná, Timbú, and other peoples occupied the Paraná River littoral with fishing-based economies.

920.name: Inca Expansion and Early European Contact
920.description: The Inca Empire's southward expansion into northwestern Argentina (Kollasuyu), creating the southernmost frontier of Tawantinsuyu, followed by the first Spanish explorations, the founding of cities, and the beginning of colonial conquest.

sub_clusters.name: Inca Expansion into Kollasuyu
sub_clusters.description: Under Topa Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac, the Inca Empire expanded into northwestern Argentina, incorporating Diaguita and Huarpe peoples into the quarter of Kollasuyu. The Incas built roads, tambos (way stations), and administrative centers, including Shincal de Quimivil, though Diaguita resistance limited full control.
key_events: Topa Inca Yupanqui conquers northwestern Argentina c. 1480
Shincal de Quimivil established as Inca administrative center

sub_clusters.name: Spanish Expeditions and the Founding of Cities
sub_clusters.description: Juan Díaz de Solís reached the Río de la Plata in 1516; Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires in 1536 but starvation and indigenous attacks forced abandonment. Spanish colonization proceeded from the north (Santiago del Estero, 1553) and from Chile. Juan de Garay re-founded Buenos Aires in 1580, establishing the permanent settlement.
key_events: Díaz de Solís reaches Río de la Plata — 1516
First founding of Buenos Aires by Mendoza — 1536 (abandoned)
Juan de Garay re-founds Buenos Aires — 1580

930.name: Colonial Argentina and the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata
930.description: Three centuries of Spanish colonial rule — from Buenos Aires's re-founding through the creation of the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata in 1776 — encompassing the Jesuit Missions, the rise of contraband trade, the Bourbon Reforms, and the British invasions that catalyzed criollo self-confidence.

sub_clusters.name: Jesuit Missions among the Guaraní
sub_clusters.description: The Jesuit Reductions in Misiones organized over 100,000 Guaraní into self-sufficient mission communities with churches, workshops, and farms. These 'republics' protected Guaraní from slave raiders (bandeirantes) but were dismantled when Charles III expelled the Jesuits in 1767. The ruins of San Ignacio Miní are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
key_events: First Jesuit Reductions established in Misiones — 1609
Expulsion of the Jesuits from Spanish territories — 1767

sub_clusters.name: Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata and Bourbon Reforms
sub_clusters.description: Spain created the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata in 1776, elevating Buenos Aires from a peripheral outpost to a viceregal capital encompassing present-day Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Bolivia. The Bourbon Reforms liberalized trade, and Buenos Aires boomed as an export center for hides, tallow, and salted meat.
key_events: Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata created — 1776
Free trade regulation opens Buenos Aires port — 1778

sub_clusters.name: British Invasions and Criollo Awakening
sub_clusters.description: The British captured Buenos Aires in 1806 and Montevideo in 1807, but criollo militias led by Santiago de Liniers expelled the invaders without Spanish military help. This experience of self-defense galvanized criollo political consciousness and demonstrated that local forces could govern independently, directly setting the stage for the May Revolution.
key_events: British capture Buenos Aires — June 1806; reconquered by Liniers — August 1806
Second British invasion repelled — July 1807

940.name: Independence, Civil Wars, and National Organization
940.description: The May Revolution of 1810, formal independence in 1816, San Martín's liberation campaigns, decades of civil war between Unitarios and Federales, the Rosas dictatorship, the Battle of Caseros, and the constitutional consolidation of the Argentine Republic.

sub_clusters.name: The May Revolution and Independence
sub_clusters.description: The Revolución de Mayo (May 25, 1810) deposed the Spanish viceroy and established a criollo junta in Buenos Aires. The Congress of Tucumán formally declared independence on July 9, 1816. General José de San Martín organized the Army of the Andes and crossed the Andes to liberate Chile (1817) and Peru (1821).
key_events: May Revolution (Revolución de Mayo) — May 25, 1810
Declaration of independence at Tucumán — July 9, 1816
San Martín crosses the Andes — January 1817

sub_clusters.name: Unitarios vs. Federales: The Civil Wars
sub_clusters.description: Decades of violent conflict between the Unitarios (centralists favoring Buenos Aires) and Federales (provincial autonomists). Juan Manuel de Rosas dominated as Federal caudillo of Buenos Aires Province (1829–1852), ruling through a network of terror (the Mazorca), controlling foreign affairs, and blocking constitutional organization until his defeat at the Battle of Caseros.
key_events: Rosas assumes power as governor of Buenos Aires — 1829
Battle of Caseros — Urquiza defeats Rosas, February 3, 1852

sub_clusters.name: Constitutional Organization and the Conquest of the Desert
sub_clusters.description: The Constitution of 1853 established a federal republic. Buenos Aires seceded (1852–1861) before rejoining after the Battle of Pavón. President Julio Argentino Roca's Conquest of the Desert (1879–1880) militarily subjugated the Mapuche and Tehuelche peoples of Patagonia and the Pampas, opening vast lands for European settlement and cattle ranching.
key_events: Argentine Constitution adopted — May 1, 1853
Conquest of the Desert under General Roca — 1879–1880

940.name: The Generation of '80 and the Great Immigration
940.description: Argentina's golden age of export-led growth — the Generación del Ochenta's liberal oligarchic republic, massive European immigration that transformed Argentine society, the rise of the agricultural export economy (beef, wheat), and the emergence of working-class politics and the Radical Civic Union.

sub_clusters.name: The Oligarchic Republic and Export Boom
sub_clusters.description: Under the Generation of '80, Argentina became one of the world's wealthiest nations through beef and grain exports to Britain. Buenos Aires was federalized (1880), railroads expanded across the Pampas, and the landed oligarchy controlled politics through electoral fraud. Argentina attracted more European immigrants per capita than the United States.
key_events: Buenos Aires federalized as national capital — 1880
Argentina becomes world's leading grain and beef exporter by 1900

sub_clusters.name: Mass European Immigration and Social Change
sub_clusters.description: Between 1880 and 1930, over 6 million European immigrants (primarily Italian and Spanish) arrived in Argentina, making it the second-largest immigration destination in the Americas. This transformed Buenos Aires into a cosmopolitan metropolis, gave rise to tango culture in the conventillos (tenements), and created new working and middle classes that demanded political inclusion.
key_events: Sáenz Peña Law establishes universal male suffrage and secret ballot — 1912
Tango emerges from Buenos Aires working-class neighborhoods 1880s–1900s

950.name: Radicalism, Peronism, and Political Instability
950.description: The Radical era under Yrigoyen, the 1930 coup that inaugurated decades of political instability, the rise of Juan Domingo Perón and Eva Perón as transformative figures in Argentine politics, import-substitution industrialization, and the cycle of coups and proscriptions.

sub_clusters.name: The Radical Era and the Década Infame
sub_clusters.description: Hipólito Yrigoyen became the first president elected under universal male suffrage (1916). The Semana Trágica (1919) and Patagonia Rebelde (1921) revealed class tensions. The 1930 coup against Yrigoyen inaugurated the Década Infame (Infamous Decade) of conservative fraud, and Argentina maintained controversial neutrality during most of World War II.
key_events: Yrigoyen elected president — first under Sáenz Peña Law, 1916
Military coup ousts Yrigoyen — September 6, 1930

sub_clusters.name: Perón, Evita, and the Rise of Justicialism
sub_clusters.description: Colonel Juan Domingo Perón rose to power through the 1943 military government, was elected president in 1946 with massive working-class support, and — alongside his wife Eva 'Evita' Perón — built the Peronist/Justicialist movement that dominated Argentine politics for decades. The Peróns championed workers' rights, women's suffrage (1947), and state-led industrialization. Evita's death in 1952 and economic decline led to Perón's overthrow in the Revolución Libertadora of 1955.
key_events: October 17, 1945 — workers rally to free Perón, founding moment of Peronism
Eva Perón dies — July 26, 1952
Revolución Libertadora overthrows Perón — September 1955

sub_clusters.name: Proscription, Instability, and the Return of Perón
sub_clusters.description: Peronism was banned (1955–1973), producing chronic political instability with alternating civilian and military governments. The Cordobazo uprising (1969) shook the military dictatorship. Perón returned from exile in 1973 and was elected president again, but died in 1974, leaving his third wife Isabel as president amid escalating violence between left-wing guerrillas (Montoneros, ERP) and right-wing death squads (Triple A).
key_events: Cordobazo workers' and students' uprising — May 29, 1969
Perón returns from exile and wins presidency — 1973; dies July 1, 1974

950.name: The Dirty War, Malvinas/Falklands, and Democratic Restoration
950.description: The military junta's Proceso de Reorganización Nacional (1976–1983), the state terrorism of the Dirty War with up to 30,000 disappeared, the Falklands/Malvinas War of 1982 that hastened the junta's collapse, and the restoration of democracy under Raúl Alfonsín.

sub_clusters.name: The Proceso and the Dirty War
sub_clusters.description: The military junta led by Jorge Videla, Roberto Viola, and Leopoldo Galtieri waged a 'dirty war' (guerra sucia) against suspected leftists, using secret detention centers (including the ESMA), torture, and death flights. An estimated 30,000 people were 'disappeared' (desaparecidos). The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began their silent protests in 1977, becoming an international symbol of human rights resistance.
key_events: Military coup establishes the Proceso — March 24, 1976
Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo begin marching — April 30, 1977
1978 FIFA World Cup held in Argentina amid state terrorism

sub_clusters.name: The Falklands/Malvinas War
sub_clusters.description: General Galtieri invaded the British-held Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas) on April 2, 1982, seeking to rally nationalist support for the faltering junta. Britain dispatched a naval task force and recaptured the islands after 74 days of fighting. Argentina's defeat (649 Argentine dead) discredited the military regime and accelerated the transition to democracy.
key_events: Argentine forces invade Falklands/Malvinas — April 2, 1982
British forces recapture Port Stanley — June 14, 1982

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Restoration under Alfonsín
sub_clusters.description: Raúl Alfonsín (UCR) won the 1983 election and presided over the democratic transition. The CONADEP commission documented the Dirty War's crimes in the landmark report Nunca Más (Never Again), and the Trial of the Juntas (1985) convicted top military leaders — an unprecedented act in Latin America. Hyperinflation ultimately undermined Alfonsín's presidency.
key_events: Alfonsín elected president — October 30, 1983
Trial of the Juntas — top military leaders convicted, 1985

960.name: Neoliberalism, the 2001 Crisis, and Kirchnerism
960.description: Carlos Menem's neoliberal reforms and convertibility (peso-dollar parity), the catastrophic 2001 economic crisis that saw five presidents in two weeks, the Kirchnerist era under Néstor and Cristina Kirchner with its mix of social spending, commodity-boom growth, and polarizing populism.

sub_clusters.name: Menem, Convertibility, and Neoliberal Reform
sub_clusters.description: Carlos Menem (1989–1999) implemented sweeping neoliberal reforms: peso-dollar convertibility (1991), mass privatization, trade liberalization, and deregulation. Initial stability gave way to rising unemployment, deindustrialization, and crushing external debt. The AMIA bombing (1994) killed 85 and remained Argentina's worst terrorist attack.
key_events: Convertibility Plan pegs peso to dollar — 1991
AMIA Jewish community center bombing — July 18, 1994

sub_clusters.name: The 2001 Crisis: ¡Que Se Vayan Todos!
sub_clusters.description: Argentina suffered the largest sovereign debt default in history (December 2001), the corralito froze bank deposits, and mass protests (cacerolazos) erupted with the cry '¡Que se vayan todos!' (Out with them all!). Five presidents served in two weeks. Unemployment reached 25%, poverty exceeded 50%, and the peso lost two-thirds of its value. The crisis became a defining event of anti-globalization discourse.
key_events: Argentina defaults on $132 billion in sovereign debt — December 2001
Five presidents in two weeks — December 2001

sub_clusters.name: Kirchnerism and the Commodity Boom
sub_clusters.description: Néstor Kirchner (2003–2007) and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner (2007–2015) presided over economic recovery fueled by soybean exports, expanded social programs, annulled amnesty laws for Dirty War crimes enabling new trials, nationalized YPF, and pursued a confrontational media and foreign policy. The era produced deep political polarization between Kirchnerism and its opponents.

960.name: Contemporary Argentina: From Macri to Milei
960.description: Mauricio Macri's center-right government and return to international markets, the return of Kirchnerism under Alberto Fernández, the COVID-19 pandemic, persistent inflation, and the dramatic 2023 election of libertarian outsider Javier Milei with his agenda of radical economic reform.

sub_clusters.name: The Macri Era and Return to the IMF
sub_clusters.description: Mauricio Macri (Cambiemos coalition) won in 2015 as the first non-Peronist/non-Radical elected president in decades. He liberalized the economy, settled with holdout creditors, and obtained a record $57 billion IMF loan (2018), but rising inflation and peso devaluation eroded his support.

sub_clusters.name: Milei and Libertarian Disruption
sub_clusters.description: Javier Milei, a libertarian economist and political outsider, won the 2023 presidential election with promises to dollarize the economy, close the Central Bank, and slash the state. His presidency represents a radical break in Argentine politics, reflecting deep voter frustration with chronic inflation exceeding 200% annually and decades of economic mismanagement.
key_events: Javier Milei elected president — November 19, 2023
Annual inflation exceeds 200% — the highest in three decades

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
